Shep Hyken · Where We Left Off

Magic. Mediocrity. Misery.

The May framework in one slide. Every visit, call, text, and invoice lands in exactly one. Most companies obsess over Misery. The dangerous one is Mediocrity.

Moment of

Misery

Falls below expectation. The customer feels something. They tell people. They do not come back.

"Never again."
Moment of

Mediocrity

Meets the baseline. The customer feels nothing memorable. The silent killer of service businesses.

"Fine."
Moment of

Magic

Exceeds expectation. The customer notices. They tell their neighbor. They book the next visit before you ask.

"Wow."
Shep Hyken · The Moment of Magic, one step further
In May, the customer said
"Please come back."
Today, the customer says
"I'll recommend you to my neighbor."

A Moment of Magic earns the next visit. A Moment of Magic that lingers earns the next customer. Same tech. Same doorstep. The difference is what we do in the seventy-two hours after we leave.

The Pivot

The Lens Turns to What Lingers.

In February we worked on what happens between us. In May we worked on what happens at the doorstep. Today we work on what happens after the truck pulls away. The customer stands in their kitchen. The invoice is paid. The tech is three streets over. And something is still there. A feeling. A great story forming. A name they will either repeat to a neighbor or never say again. The aftertaste is the only part of the visit the customer keeps. Lead for what lingers, and your customers start selling for you. Ignore it, and every visit is a coin flip.

The Aftertaste

The Moment of Magic, One Week Later.

Hyken's three states from May, measured after we leave. The customer does not remember the visit. They remember what the visit left behind.

Misery leaves it

Bitter

They are still talking about it. To the neighbor. On the review site. In the group text. The story has our name in it and we are the villain.

"I would warn you."
Mediocrity leaves it

Bland

They cannot remember who came out. They will shop the next job. We were fine, and fine is forgotten by Thursday.

"Some company. They were fine."
Magic leaves it

Sweet

They repeat the tech's name. They bring us up unprompted. They defend us when a neighbor complains about their guy. We became part of their story.

"You have to call ABC."
The Ladder

Satisfied Is Not the Finish Line.

A satisfied customer got what they paid for. That is the price of admission, not the prize. Advocacy is three rungs up, and every rung is a Moment of Magic you choose to create after the work is done.

Rung One

Satisfied

The work was done right, on time. They feel nothing in particular.

Silent.
→
Rung Two

Loyal

They call us again without shopping. They trust the name.

"I wouldn't call anyone else. See you guys next time."
→
Rung Three

Advocate

They tell the neighbor. They leave the review. They defend us.

"I'll recommend you to my neighbor."
→
Rung Four

Legacy

Their kids call us. The whole street calls us. Our name is part of the neighborhood.

"We have always used ABC."
The Mapping

Four Pillars. Four Things That Linger.

In May you mapped each pillar to a Moment of Magic. Today you hear what your customer says about each one a month later, when you are not in the room.

01 Reliable Service

"They show up when they say they will."

The lingering feeling of certainty. They stop taking the whole day off for us. They stop calling to confirm. Trust is the aftertaste of reliability.

02 Responsible Practices

"They did it right, not just fast."

The lingering feeling of being protected. The right product, the right dose, the gate closed, the dog noticed. They stop worrying about what we left behind.

03 Personal Connection

"Can you send the same tech?"

The lingering feeling of being known. They remember a name, and they ask for it. A person, not a ticket, in both directions.

04 Excellence with Integrity

"I just call ABC for everything."

The lingering feeling of safety. They never wonder if the invoice is honest or the work is real. The legacy pillar. It is only earned by what we do after something breaks.

Hear It From Him

Where "Ladies and Gentlemen" Came From.

Edited clip · 3 min 27 sec

Listen for one word: respect.

Two stories, back to back. The essay he wrote at sixteen and what it taught him about defining yourself. Then the day he left home at fourteen, the manager who told him he was there to be a servant, and the maître d' who proved otherwise. Listen for the line: "If we do not, we sentence ourselves to be servants."

01 Principle One

Dignity at the Doorstep.

Every individual is treated with dignity. Not the ones who earned it. Every one.

After Horst Schulze

The customer in the mobile home and the customer in the Highland Park mansion. The customer who is rude on the phone. The CSR on her fortieth call. The new tech on his first ride-along. Dignity is not a reward for good behavior. It is the standard we carry in the truck. And it starts inside the hive. Ladies and Gentlemen cannot serve Ladies and Gentlemen if we do not treat our own people that way first.

02 Principle Two

The Empowered Yes.

The person closest to the customer has the authority to make it right, right now, without a phone call. We introduced it in May and sent you home with one question: what is DFW's number? Today it becomes a policy conversation, not a poster.

$2,000

Per employee. Per guest. No permission.

The Ritz-Carlton number. Not because problems cost that much. Because the customer standing on the driveway does not have time for us to find a manager.

Ninety Days Later

The Empowered Yes, Revisited.

The same Tuesday afternoon in DFW, told twice. The only thing that changes is whether the tech knows his number.

Tuesday, 4:55 PM · A Permission Culture

"Let me check with my manager."

The tech nicked a sprinkler line. He knows how to fix it. He also knows he is not allowed to comp a forty-dollar repair without a call. So he calls. The manager is in a meeting. The customer waits on the driveway, arms folded, and hears the word "policy" twice before anyone says "sorry."

Aftertaste: "They had to ask permission to do the right thing."
Tuesday, 4:55 PM · A Yes Culture

"Already handled. My mistake."

Same nick. Same tech. He knows his number. He fixes the line, tells the customer what he did and why, and knocks the repair off the invoice before she asks. He mentions it at the Tuesday meeting and gets a round of applause, not a write-up.

Aftertaste: "That guy owned it. Ask for him next time."
03 Principle Three · From Shep Hyken

The Recovery Paradox.

A customer who has a problem, and watches us fix it well, ends up more loyal than a customer who never had a problem at all. Researchers have measured it for thirty years. Hyken built a career on it. Most home services companies have never heard of it.

"They were fine."
No problem,
no recovery
"Never again."
Problem,
poor recovery
"You have to call ABC."
Problem,
great recovery
Recovery

Four Moves. In Order. Every Time.

Today a miss in DFW usually ends at the fix. Nobody calls first, nobody calls after, and the customer decides what it meant. Here is the sequence your whole team can run without you in the room.

01 Within the Hour

Acknowledge

Surface it before the customer does. Say what happened in plain words, in their words. The clock starts the moment we know, not the moment they call.

02 Human Voice

Apologize

Pick up the phone. Use their name. Own the impact, not the excuse. They do not care about the backorder. They care they took the morning off.

03 The Empowered Yes

Act

Make the remedy bigger than the problem, and make it now. This is where the dollar amount either exists or it does not.

04 Three Days Later

Aftercare

The call nobody expects. "Just checking that it held." The aftertaste is written here, not at the fix. This is the move most companies skip.

From Hyken

Three Moments of Magic Nobody Sees.

In May the Magic happened at the doorstep with the customer watching. The Q3 Magic happens after we leave, when nobody is watching. That is exactly why it lingers.

Magic Moment · Day Three

The Callback

"Just making sure it held." Sixty seconds. No upsell. The customer has never once received this call from a home services company. Now they have.

Anticipate, after the fact.
Magic Moment · The Miss

The Recovery

We broke it, we said so first, we fixed it bigger than we broke it, and we called three days later. The customer tells that story for a decade.

Communicate, when it hurts.
Magic Moment · The Referral

The Thank-You

A neighbor calls because of them. We call them back to say so, by name, from the tech who did the work. Advocates who feel honored advocate again.

Close the loop, twice.

A Suggested Rhythm

Four Places the Language Could Live.

A suggestion, not a mandate. Pick the ones that fit your team, then put the words on the agenda by name so nobody has to remember to bring them up.

Daily · Huddle

Magic Moment of the Day

60 seconds

One named Moment of Magic from yesterday. Who did it, what they did, which pillar it served. Name names. Make heroes.

Weekly · Team Meeting

The Tuesday Story and the Recovery Replay

10 minutes

One customer story someone repeated about us. One miss, walked through Acknowledge, Apologize, Act, Aftercare. No blame. Just the replay.

Monthly · Manager Meeting

The Aftertaste Review

20 minutes

Reviews, referrals, and recoveries from the month, read aloud. One Dignity Check answer from the front line. What did we leave behind?

Quarterly · The Hive

The Card and the Story

Each quarter

Your 90-day card, read aloud, with the true story it produced. Q3 today. Marble Falls in Q4. The rhythm that holds the year together.

The Call to Action
Leave It Sweeter.

A worker bee lives about six weeks. The honey it leaves behind never spoils. Picture a Tuesday in December. Your huddle opens with a tech's name. A customer in Plano asks for him by name. A review mentions the callback. A neighbor calls because of it. Leave every home, every call, and every teammate a little sweeter than you found them, until the customer says it for you: "I'll recommend you to my neighbor."
